{
  "findings": [
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go",
      "line": 116,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "Denial cache key is not scoped by identity type",
      "body": "In Service.Check, permDenialKey is built from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder, but not the identity type. validateSubject permits anonymous and render-service identities, and both can have the identifier \"0\" (e.g. anonymous:0 and render:0). A denied anonymous check will therefore write a negative cache entry under the same key used by a render:0 check for the same resource. A subsequent renderer check can hit that denial cache entry and return Allowed:false before getRendererPermissions is evaluated, even though the renderer is hard-coded to read all dashboards/folders. Similar cross-identity denials are possible between other identity types if identifiers are not globally unique. The denial cache key should include the identity type, or renderer/anonymous checks should bypass this denial cache."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go",
      "line": 31,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "Denial cache key concatenation can collide",
      "body": "userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with underscores and no escaping. If any of these fields can contain underscores (for example user-supplied dashboard/folder UIDs), distinct authorization checks can produce the same cache key. For example, name=\"a\" and parent=\"b_c\" produces the same key as name=\"a_b\" and parent=\"c\". Because this cache stores negative authorization decisions, such a collision can cause a denial for one resource to incorrectly apply to another resource. Use an unambiguous separator/encoding, or hash length-prefixed fields."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go",
      "line": 154,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "data",
      "title": "Negative caching can continue denying access after permission is granted",
      "body": "Service.Check stores a denial in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds) whenever the database check denies access. There is no invalidation when permissions are added or changed. If a permission is granted immediately after a denial—for example during dashboard/folder creation, permission propagation, or a read-before-write race—subsequent checks can hit the denial cache and keep rejecting the user until the TTL expires. This can reintroduce the same inability to access newly created resources that this PR is trying to fix."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go",
      "line": 982,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "test_gap",
      "title": "Denial-cache test does not actually seed an allowed cached permission",
      "body": "In TestService_CacheCheck, the subtest \"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry\" claims to prove that the denial cache overrides cached permissions, but it seeds permCache with map[string]bool{\"dashboards:uid:dash1\": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no permission, so the check would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored. To verify that an explicit denial entry overrides a cached allow, the test should seed the permission cache with true for that scope."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go",
      "line": 124,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Errors from cached identity lookup are treated as cache misses",
      "body": "getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors from GetUserIdentifiers for user/service-account subjects, but Service.Check only proceeds with the cached path when err == nil and otherwise falls through as though it were a cache miss. It then calls getIdentityPermissions, which repeats GetUserIdentifiers. This can duplicate database work during failures, add latency, and emit misleading cache-miss metrics instead of distinguishing cache lookup failures from ordinary cache misses."
    }
  ]
}

findings.title: Denial cache key is not scoped by identity type
findings.body: In Service.Check, permDenialKey is built from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder, but not the identity type. validateSubject permits anonymous and render-service identities, and both can have the identifier "0" (e.g. anonymous:0 and render:0). A denied anonymous check will therefore write a negative cache entry under the same key used by a render:0 check for the same resource. A subsequent renderer check can hit that denial cache entry and return Allowed:false before getRendererPermissions is evaluated, even though the renderer is hard-coded to read all dashboards/folders. Similar cross-identity denials are possible between other identity types if identifiers are not globally unique. The denial cache key should include the identity type, or renderer/anonymous checks should bypass this denial cache.

findings.title: Denial cache key concatenation can collide
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with underscores and no escaping. If any of these fields can contain underscores (for example user-supplied dashboard/folder UIDs), distinct authorization checks can produce the same cache key. For example, name="a" and parent="b_c" produces the same key as name="a_b" and parent="c". Because this cache stores negative authorization decisions, such a collision can cause a denial for one resource to incorrectly apply to another resource. Use an unambiguous separator/encoding, or hash length-prefixed fields.

findings.title: Negative caching can continue denying access after permission is granted
findings.body: Service.Check stores a denial in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds) whenever the database check denies access. There is no invalidation when permissions are added or changed. If a permission is granted immediately after a denial—for example during dashboard/folder creation, permission propagation, or a read-before-write race—subsequent checks can hit the denial cache and keep rejecting the user until the TTL expires. This can reintroduce the same inability to access newly created resources that this PR is trying to fix.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually seed an allowed cached permission
findings.body: In TestService_CacheCheck, the subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" claims to prove that the denial cache overrides cached permissions, but it seeds permCache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no permission, so the check would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored. To verify that an explicit denial entry overrides a cached allow, the test should seed the permission cache with true for that scope.

findings.title: Errors from cached identity lookup are treated as cache misses
findings.body: getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors from GetUserIdentifiers for user/service-account subjects, but Service.Check only proceeds with the cached path when err == nil and otherwise falls through as though it were a cache miss. It then calls getIdentityPermissions, which repeats GetUserIdentifiers. This can duplicate database work during failures, add latency, and emit misleading cache-miss metrics instead of distinguishing cache lookup failures from ordinary cache misses.
